method: TechFlow editorial assessment for a typical product team building web/mobile backends in 2026. Rings describe how confidently we would start a new project with the item today — not how good the technology is in the abstract. Re-assessed quarterly; disagreement is expected and welcome.

entries.note: Default for new JavaScript codebases; the ecosystem assumes it.
Still the most widely deployed UI library; server components have matured.
Safe default for API servers and tooling; runtime alternatives exist but the ecosystem is here.
Earns its complexity for many-client, many-shape data needs; overkill for a single web app.
Excellent for service-to-service calls with strict contracts; browser story still needs a proxy.
The default public API style; boring in the best way.
Containers are the unit of deployment almost everywhere.
Right when you run many services and have platform capacity; a burden for a small team with one app.
Reverse proxy, TLS termination and static serving with decades of production mileage.
Put one in front of anything public; cheap latency and origin protection.
Object storage is the durable, cheap default for files, backups and data lakes.
Metrics standard; pair with a dashboard and tracing for full observability.
Logs, metrics and traces from day one — retrofitting is far more expensive.
The default relational database; JSONB, extensions and managed offerings cover most needs.
Mature and everywhere; choose it when your team or platform already runs it.
Cache, session store, counters and pub/sub — nearly every backend ends up with one.
Still excellent for pure multi-threaded caching, but Redis covers the same job plus more.
Unmatched for durable event streams; heavy to operate for a team without streaming needs.
Pragmatic task queue and routing broker when you do not need a replayable log.
Good fit for document-shaped, schema-flexible data; think twice for relational domains.
Superb at scale with known access patterns; painful when queries are not known upfront.
The search default; keep the source of truth elsewhere and treat the index as derived.
The first performance lever to pull; low risk when TTLs are set.
The reliable way to publish events alongside database writes.
Mandatory once you call anything over a network you do not control.
Design every mutating endpoint to be safely retried.
Powerful decoupling; needs observability and idempotency to stay debuggable.
Solves real read/write asymmetry; frequently adopted where a good index would do.
Necessary for cross-service transactions; prefer avoiding the distributed transaction first.
Organisational scaling tool; start with a modular monolith unless you already have many teams.
Best default architecture for a new product: clear modules, one deployable.
Fast, but data loss on cache failure is easy to underestimate.
Underused: simpler than WebSocket for server → client streams such as AI token output.
The standard for bidirectional real-time; plan for scaling connections across servers.
